302.title: A very narrow bridge
302.hook: Rebbe Nachman: the whole world is a very narrow bridge, and the main thing is not to be afraid
302.howItsDone: The song Kol ha-olam kulo, set to Rebbe Nachman's words, is sung at weddings, camps, memorials and gatherings; Breslov Hasidim study his teachings in Likutei Moharan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a tailor made his accounting with God on Yom Kippur. Your line was let's call it even. Did you tell one honest truth, kindly? Day three hundred two.

Go to almost any Jewish wedding, summer camp or youth group, and at some point people put their arms around each other's shoulders and sway, singing a slow Hebrew song. Kol ha-olam kulo, gesher tzar me'od. The whole world is a very narrow bridge. And the main thing is not to be afraid at all. Millions of people know the tune. Far fewer know where the words come from: a Hasidic master who died young, who wrote openly about sadness, and whose actual words are a little different from the song. Today: the bridge.
screen: `ARMS AROUND SHOULDERS, SWAYING.` → `THE WHOLE WORLD IS A NARROW BRIDGE.` → `WHERE DO THE WORDS COME FROM?`

segments.voice: Rebbe Nachman of Breslov was born in 1772, a great-grandson of the Baal Shem Tov, whose stories we've been hearing. He lived in Ukraine and died at thirty-eight, in the town of Uman. His student Nathan wrote down his teachings in a great book called Likutei Moharan. In one passage, Rebbe Nachman says, roughly: know that a person has to cross a very, very narrow bridge, and the rule and the main thing is not to frighten yourself at all. Nearly two hundred years later, a songwriter turned that into the song, and changed it a little on the way. The song says the whole world is the bridge. And the song says, don't be afraid. The original is subtler. The Hebrew verb is reflexive: don't make yourself afraid. Fear will come. It comes to everyone standing over a drop. What you can refuse to do is feed it, to stand there frightening yourself with every way you might fall. Notice what the teaching doesn't say. It doesn't say the bridge is wide. It doesn't say you won't wobble. It says the path really is narrow, and you still have to cross it. Rebbe Nachman knew this from inside. He spoke often of his own heaviness of spirit, and he also taught that it is a great mitzvah to be joyful always. Not because life is easy, but because joy is how you keep walking. So the bridge isn't a promise of safety. It's permission to be scared and move anyway.
screen: `NACHMAN OF BRESLOV, 1772–1810.` · `A VERY, VERY NARROW BRIDGE.` · `DON'T MAKE YOURSELF AFRAID.` · `SCARED, AND WALKING ANYWAY.` · then, large: `NOT AFRAID AT ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one step in spite of fear. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you've been avoiding because it scares you. A phone call. A doctor's appointment. An apology. A conversation. Don't try to stop being afraid of it. Just notice the fear, and notice when you start frightening yourself with stories about how it'll go. Now picture only the first step. Not the whole bridge. One plank. See yourself taking it. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to take it. The bell holds the time.
A very narrow bridge. Rebbe Nachman's picture of life: the way across is narrow, and the main thing is not to make yourself afraid.
Your line: not afraid at all. Today, when fear shows up, don't argue with it. Just stop feeding it, and take the first step. Day three hundred two.

303.title: The lost princess
303.hook: Rebbe Nachman's tale of a viceroy who searches for years for a lost princess
303.howItsDone: Rebbe Nachman's thirteen tales, collected as Sippurei Ma'asiyot, are read and studied by Breslov Hasidim and many others, often with commentaries that explain their hidden meanings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rebbe Nachman's very narrow bridge. Your line was not afraid at all. Did you take one step? Today, the same rebbe tells a story, the first of his famous tales. Day three hundred three.

Rebbe Nachman didn't only teach. Near the end of his short life he started telling stories. Fairy tales, really: kings and princesses, giants, deserts, enchanted palaces. His followers were puzzled at first. Why is our rebbe telling us bedtime stories? But he told them these stories hid deep things, and his student Nathan wrote them down. The first one is about a king who says one careless sentence in anger, and loses the person he loves most. Today: the lost princess.
screen: `A REBBE TELLS FAIRY TALES.` → `KINGS, GIANTS, PALACES.` → `ONE CARELESS SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the story, in short strokes. A king has a daughter he loves dearly. One day, angry with her, he blurts out: may the not-good take you. The next morning, she's gone. The king is heartbroken. His viceroy, his second-in-command, asks for a servant, a horse and some money, and sets out to find her. He searches for years. At last he finds her, held in a strange palace. She tells him how to free her: choose a place, long for her for a whole year, and on the last day, fast. On the last day, he sees an apple, eats it, and falls into a deep sleep. He fails. She gives him a second chance: this time, don't drink. He finds a spring, drinks, and sleeps for seventy years. When he wakes, she's been taken farther away. All that's left is her kerchief, with a message written in her tears: now look for me on a mountain of gold, in a castle of pearl. So he gets up. He keeps searching. The tale follows him through deserts and giants. And its last line is strange: how he freed her, the story doesn't tell. But in the end, he freed her. Breslov teachers read the princess as the Divine Presence in exile, and the viceroy as every person who has lost something holy and is trying to find it again. He isn't a hero because he never fails. He fails twice, badly. He's a hero because the story always says the same thing next: and he kept searching.
screen: `ONE ANGRY SENTENCE.` · `YEARS OF SEARCHING.` · `AN APPLE. A SPRING. SEVENTY YEARS.` · `A MESSAGE WRITTEN IN TEARS.` · then, large: `KEEP SEARCHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep searching for one good thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of something good you once had and have lost track of. A friendship. A habit. A sense of wonder. A way of praying. Don't scold yourself for falling asleep on it. The viceroy slept seventy years and still got up. Just ask: where might I look for it now? One place. One small first step. If you pray, you can ask for help finding it. The bell holds the time.
The lost princess. Rebbe Nachman's first tale: a viceroy who fails, sleeps, wakes, and keeps looking until he finds what was lost.
Your line: keep searching. Today, when you notice you've let something good slip, don't give up on it. Take one step back toward it. Day three hundred three.

304.title: The turkey prince
304.hook: a prince thinks he's a turkey, and a sage sits under the table with him
304.howItsDone: The turkey prince parable is retold in Breslov circles, Jewish schools and sermons, often as a lesson in patience and in meeting people where they are.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lost princess and the viceroy who kept failing and kept looking. Your line was keep searching. Did you take one step back toward something good? Day three hundred four.

Think about the last time you tried to help someone who didn't want help. A friend spiraling. A teenager who wouldn't talk. A parent refusing to see the doctor. You stood over them with good advice, and the more right you were, the more they dug in. Rebbe Nachman told a short, funny parable about exactly that. It involves a royal family, a dining table, and a prince who has decided he is a turkey. It's one of the most loved stories in the Breslov tradition, and it's still retold in classrooms and therapy offices.
screen: `HELPING SOMEONE WHO WON'T BE HELPED.` → `THE MORE RIGHT YOU ARE…` → `A PRINCE WHO THINKS HE'S A TURKEY.`

segments.voice: A prince goes mad. He decides he's a turkey. He takes off his clothes, crawls under the table, and pecks at crumbs on the floor. The king calls every doctor in the land. They argue with him, they order him, they try every cure. Nothing. Then a wise man comes and says: let me try. He takes off his own clothes, crawls under the table, and starts pecking crumbs. The prince stares at him. Who are you? A turkey, says the wise man. And you? Also a turkey. So they sit together, two turkeys, and become friends. After a while, the wise man asks for a shirt. The prince is shocked. The wise man says: who says a turkey can't wear a shirt? You can wear a shirt and still be a turkey. So they both put on shirts. Later, trousers. Later, real food from the table. You can eat good food and still be a turkey. Then one day, the wise man says: you can sit at the table and still be a turkey. And little by little, the prince lives like a prince again. The Yiddish word for turkey is hindik, and Breslov Hasidim still call this the hindik story. Teachers read it on more than one level. On the plain level, it's about how to help: don't shout from the chair. Get under the table. Start where the other person actually is, and move one step at a time. On a deeper level, many read it about the soul: nobody jumps from the floor to the table in one leap.
screen: `A PRINCE UNDER THE TABLE.` · `THE WISE MAN: ALSO A TURKEY.` · `A SHIRT, THEN TROUSERS, THEN FOOD.` · `ONE STEP AT A TIME.` · then, large: `SIT UNDER THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: meet someone where they are. Settle, and breathe. Think of one person you've been trying to change, or fix, or talk sense into. Now, in your mind, stop standing over them. Get down to where they are. What does the world look like from under their table? What are they afraid of? What would make them feel a little less alone? Don't plan a speech. Look for one small thing you could share with them, the way the wise man shared the floor. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
The turkey prince. Rebbe Nachman's parable of a wise man who got under the table, and brought a prince back one small step at a time.
Your line: sit under the table. Today, before you give someone advice, spend a minute where they are. Ask one question and just listen. Day three hundred four.

305.title: Where is God?
305.hook: the Kotzker rebbe: God dwells wherever we let Him in
305.howItsDone: In the Kedushah, said aloud in the synagogue's repetition of the Amidah, the congregation proclaims Isaiah's line that the whole earth is full of God's glory; the Kotzker's saying is often quoted in sermons on sincerity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the turkey prince, and a wise man who met him on the floor. Your line was sit under the table. Did you listen before advising? Day three hundred five.

Kids ask it all the time, usually at bedtime. Where is God? Up in the sky? In the synagogue? Everywhere? Grown-ups tend to have a quick answer ready, and the quick answer is usually everywhere. It's a good answer. It's even in the Bible. But one Hasidic rebbe, famous for being fierce, blunt and impossible to please, heard that answer from a room full of learned men, and told them they had it only half right. Today: the question, and the Kotzker's reply.
screen: `A BEDTIME QUESTION.` → `THE QUICK ANSWER: EVERYWHERE.` → `ONLY HALF RIGHT?`

segments.voice: Menachem Mendel of Kotzk lived in Poland in the first half of the eighteen hundreds. He was known for a hatred of anything fake. He wanted truth, all of it, and he could be harsh about it. The story goes that he once surprised a group of learned guests with a question. Where does God live? They laughed. What a thing to ask! Isaiah already answered it. The angels call out: "the whole earth is full of His glory." God is everywhere. The rebbe answered his own question. God lives wherever people let Him in. Notice he isn't denying the verse. The whole earth may be full of glory. But a person can walk right through it and notice nothing. You can stand in a beautiful place and be entirely somewhere else, inside your phone, your worry, your pride. The Kotzker's point is that the door opens from the inside. In the prayer called the Kedushah, the congregation says Isaiah's line, and a little later asks a question from Ezekiel's vision: where is the place of His glory? Ayeh mekom kevodo. The question sits right next to the answer. Jewish tradition holds both at once. God fills the world, and God can feel absent. The Kotzker says what closes the distance isn't a map or a building. It's a person who makes room. Someone who stops pretending, and lets something larger in.
screen: `THE KOTZKER: NOTHING FAKE.` · `THE WHOLE EARTH IS FULL OF GLORY.` · `WHEREVER PEOPLE LET HIM IN.` · `AYEH: WHERE?` · then, large: `WHEREVER YOU LET HIM IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open one door inside yourself. Settle, and breathe. Notice where you're closed right now. Maybe you're rushing. Maybe you're guarded. Maybe you're carrying a grudge, or pretending everything is fine. You don't have to force anything open. Just loosen one latch. Breathe into the tight place, and leave a little room. If you pray, you can invite God in, in your own words, or with Isaiah's line. If you don't, let the room fill with whatever is good and true right here. The bell holds the time.
Where is God? The Kotzker rebbe's answer: wherever people let Him in. The earth is full of glory, and the door opens from the inside.
Your line: wherever you let him in. Today, once, when you notice you've shut down, open the door a crack. Stop, look up, and let the moment in. Day three hundred five.

306.title: The crying baby
306.hook: Shneur Zalman leaves his prayer to rock a crying baby his absorbed son never heard
306.howItsDone: Chabad Hasidim tell this story about their first and second rebbes, and it is widely retold in Jewish homes and schools as a reminder that study and prayer must never make a person deaf to others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kotzker said God lives wherever people let Him in. Your line was wherever you let him in. Did you open a door, even a crack? Day three hundred six.

You've seen it. Someone so deep in their laptop they don't hear their name called three times. A parent on the phone while a toddler tugs and tugs at their sleeve. Or maybe that someone was you. Deep focus is a gift. It's how books get written and problems get solved. But it has a shadow. Today's story is about a great scholar, lost in holy study, who missed a sound that mattered more, and about his father, who didn't.
screen: `DEEP IN THE LAPTOP.` → `A TODDLER TUGGING A SLEEVE.` → `FOCUS HAS A SHADOW.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi founded the Chabad movement at the end of the seventeen hundreds and wrote its great book, the Tanya. The story is told that he lived in a house with his son, Dov Ber, who would later lead Chabad after him. One night Dov Ber was downstairs, completely absorbed in study. In the same room, his baby fell out of the cradle and began to cry. Dov Ber didn't hear a thing. Upstairs, Shneur Zalman was deep in his own study and prayer. He heard the crying. He stopped, came down the stairs, picked the baby up, soothed the child, and laid it back in the cradle. His son never looked up. Afterward, the father spoke to him. However lofty your learning, he said, if it keeps you from hearing a child cry, something has gone wrong. Notice who is doing the teaching here. Not a critic of study. The founder of a movement built on deep, intense contemplation. He isn't saying stop learning. He's saying learning that makes you deaf to a crying child has lost its way. Jewish law has a principle that fits: saving a life, and caring for someone in real need, comes before almost everything else. The Talmud even says that welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Divine Presence, based on Abraham leaving God's company to run to three strangers. Holiness that can't hear a baby isn't finished yet.
screen: `SHNEUR ZALMAN, FOUNDER OF CHABAD.` · `A SON TOO ABSORBED TO HEAR.` · `A FATHER WHO COMES DOWNSTAIRS.` · `LEARNING THAT HEARS.` · then, large: `THE CRYING CHILD FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop for one small need. Settle, and breathe. For the next two minutes, listen. Not to your thoughts. To the room. The sounds outside. Someone in the next room. A pet. Your own body: are you thirsty, tired, tense? Let each sound register. Now think of the people around you today. Who might be tugging at your sleeve, quietly, and you haven't noticed? Pick one. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
The crying baby. Shneur Zalman stopped his own holy study to comfort a child his son never heard. Holiness that hears.
Your line: the crying child first. Today, when someone needs you while you're busy with something important, stop, and look up. The work will wait. Day three hundred six.

307.title: To know what hurts
307.hook: Moshe Leib of Sassov learned love from a peasant: how can you love me if you don't know what hurts me?
307.howItsDone: Moshe Leib of Sassov's tavern story is often told in Jewish teaching on the command to love one's neighbor, as a reminder that love means paying attention to another person's pain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shneur Zalman came downstairs for a crying baby his son never heard. Your line was the crying child first. Did you look up for someone? Day three hundred seven.

How many times have you said I love you this month? To a partner, a parent, a kid, a friend at the end of a phone call. Love you. Love you too. It's a good habit. But here's a harder question. Of the people you said it to, do you know what's hurting them right now? Not in general. Right now, this week. Today's story is about a rebbe who said he learned what love means, not from a book, but from overhearing two men in a tavern.
screen: `LOVE YOU. LOVE YOU TOO.` → `WHAT'S HURTING THEM THIS WEEK?` → `A LESSON FROM A TAVERN.`

segments.voice: Moshe Leib of Sassov was a Hasidic rebbe in Galicia in the late seventeen hundreds, remembered for his tenderness to the poor, the sick and the widowed. He used to say that he learned how to love people from a peasant. Here's how the story goes. He was at an inn where two villagers sat drinking. After a while, one turned to the other and said: tell me, do you love me? The other said: of course I love you, with all my heart. The first one said: then tell me, what hurts me? The second shrugged. How should I know what hurts you? And the first said: if you don't know what hurts me, how can you say you love me? That's it. That's the whole story. And Moshe Leib said: from that I understood that to love someone truly is to know their need, and to carry their sorrow with them. The Torah commands, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." It's easy to hear that as a feeling. The tavern turns it into a question of attention. You can't love someone's hurt away if you've never asked what it is. There's a humility in it, too. The one who said of course I love you wasn't lying. He just hadn't looked. Moshe Leib's own life, as it's remembered, was one long answer to that question: sitting with sick children, visiting widows, going where people hurt.
screen: `MOSHE LEIB OF SASSOV.` · `DO YOU LOVE ME? OF COURSE.` · `THEN WHAT HURTS ME?` · `LOVE AS ATTENTION.` · then, large: `KNOW WHAT HURTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask someone what hurts. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you love. Picture their face. Now honestly ask yourself: do I know what's hurting them right now? If you do, hold it for a moment, as if you were carrying one corner of it. If you don't, that's today's discovery. Think of how you might ask them, gently, without fixing anything. Just: how are you, really? If you pray, you can pray for what hurts them. The bell holds the time.
To know what hurts. Moshe Leib of Sassov's lesson from a tavern: if you don't know what hurts me, how can you say you love me?
Your line: know what hurts. Today, ask one person you love how they really are, and listen to the whole answer. Day three hundred seven.

308.title: If not higher (Peretz, 1900)
308.hook: a skeptic follows the rebbe of Nemirov at dawn and finds him chopping wood for a sick widow
308.howItsDone: Peretz's story is widely read in Jewish schools and retold around the High Holy Days, alongside the long Jewish tradition of giving in secret, so that the one who receives isn't shamed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moshe Leib of Sassov learned love in a tavern. Your line was know what hurts. Did you ask someone how they really are? Day three hundred eight.

Every town has a rumor about somebody. In the town of Nemirov, the rumor was about the rebbe. Every morning in the days before the High Holy Days, when the congregation gathered before dawn to say the penitential prayers, the rebbe was missing. Where was he? His followers had an answer. He goes up to heaven, of course, to plead for us. Then a visitor from Lithuania arrived, a sharp, skeptical scholar who didn't believe a word of it. And he decided to find out. Today: a famous Yiddish short story.
screen: `THE REBBE IS MISSING AT DAWN.` → `HE GOES UP TO HEAVEN.` → `A SKEPTIC DECIDES TO FIND OUT.`

segments.voice: The story was written in Yiddish in 1900 by I. L. Peretz, one of the founders of modern Yiddish literature. The skeptic, called the Litvak, hides under the rebbe's bed overnight. Before dawn, the rebbe gets up, and he doesn't put on his holy clothes. He puts on peasant clothes, boots and a big belt, and takes an axe and a rope. The Litvak follows him, shivering, out of town and into the woods. The rebbe chops down a small tree, splits it into logs, ties a bundle and carries it to a broken-down hut. Inside lies a poor, sick widow. The rebbe speaks like a peasant: I've got wood to sell, cheap. She says: I can't pay. He says: I'll trust you. You have a great and mighty God, and you don't trust Him for a few pennies? Then he kneels and lays the wood in her stove, and with each log he murmurs a line of the dawn prayers. He lights the fire, and leaves. The Litvak stays in Nemirov and becomes the rebbe's disciple. And from then on, when anyone says that at dawn the rebbe goes up to heaven, the Litvak doesn't laugh. He just adds, quietly: if not higher. That's the punch line, and the point. Helping someone in secret, without credit, without even letting her know who you are, is placed above the heavens. And it closes a week of stories: the narrow bridge, the lost princess, the turkey prince, where is God, the crying baby, what hurts, and if not higher.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help someone without telling anyone. Settle, and breathe. Think of one small, useful thing you could do today for someone who'd never know it was you. Pay for something quietly. Fix what's broken. Leave a kind note unsigned. Refill the thing everyone forgets to refill. Picture yourself doing it, and walking away without a word. Notice how much of you wants credit, and let that part rest. If you pray, you can offer it as a prayer. The bell holds the time.
If not higher. Peretz's rebbe of Nemirov didn't go up to heaven at dawn. He chopped wood for a widow in secret. Higher, said the skeptic.
Your line: if not higher. Today, do one kind thing in secret, and tell no one. Not even later. Day three hundred eight.
